b: Firouzja wins Armageddon decider, Giri cruises into Budapest final

Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri have reached the final of the Total Chess Pilot in Budapest, where they will compete for overall victory in a two-set match on Thursday and Friday. Giri secured a 2–0 victory over Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, while Firouzja needed an Armageddon decider to get past Fabiano Caruana. Wednesday's action also saw three players forfeiting their final fast classic games, including Magnus Carlsen, who repeated his controversial decision from the previous day.

Giri completed a convincing semifinal victory over Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, winning both sets of their encounter. After Tuesday's 14½–5½ success, the Dutchman scored another win in blitz and one in rapid on Wednesday, with all remaining games ending in draws. He thus entered the final fast classic encounter with a 5-point advantage, putting Vachier-Lagrave in a must-win situation.

Giri also obtained an advantage in the final game, but eventually agreed to a draw from a position of strength. He later described that decision as "a sin". The Dutch ace, one of the more outspoken players on the elite circuit, also acknowledged that he had been "quite fortunate" to beat MVL in both blitz and rapid chess on both days, as he considers the Frenchman an overall stronger player in the faster formats.
Anish Giri giving an interview | Photo: Michal Walusza

The other semifinal was considerably more closely contested. Firouzja had won Tuesday's opening set against Caruana, meaning that a draw or better on Wednesday would have been enough to advance. The Frenchman started well, winning three of the four blitz games, with Caruana taking the remaining encounter. However, the American turned the tables in the rapid section, scoring a win and a draw to move ahead on the scoreboard.

Firouzja once again questioned the tournament's scoring system, arguing that giving rapid victories four times the value of blitz wins was not an ideal arrangement. Having lost his advantage, he needed to win the fast classic encounter to avoid an Armageddon decider. Instead, he misplayed the black side of a Sicilian Alapin and lost to Caruana.
It was a tough match between two of the strongest players in the world - Alireza Firouzja and Fabiano Caruana | Photo: Michal Walusza

It was Caruana's fifth victory in twelve fast classic games in Budapest, a format that counts towards the official classical ratings. The result took him back to second place in the live rankings with 2794.2 points, exactly 7 behind Magnus Carlsen. With two more fast classic games remaining for both players, the American still has a chance to end the tournament as world number one.

Caruana's victory in the final game gave him a 15–5 win in Wednesday's set, levelling the semifinal at one set apiece and forcing Armageddon. Having scored more points across the two sets, Caruana earned the right to choose his colour and opted for Black, with draw odds.

Firouzja, however, quickly gained a pawn from the white side of an Italian Opening and went on to convert his advantage without major difficulties. The 44-move victory secured his place in the final against Giri, despite having lost Wednesday's set by a wide margin.

Hans Niemann and Jan-Krzysztof Duda will compete for fifth place after winning their respective semifinals. Niemann had little trouble against Le Quang Liem, completing a 2–0 set victory with scores of 13½–6½ and 15½–4½. The 23-year-old Californian won both fast classic games against his Vietnamese opponent and has now scored 8/12 in that format. His results have earned him 14.2 rating points, taking him back above the 2700 mark.

Duda's route to the next stage was considerably more complicated. After losing Tuesday's opening set against Ian Nepomniachtchi, the Polish grandmaster took a one-point lead in Wednesday's blitz section. The two players then exchanged rapid victories, leaving Nepomniachtchi needing a win in the fast classic game to avoid the possibility of a decider. Instead, Duda won that encounter, forcing Armageddon.

Unlike Caruana in the title bracket, Nepomniachtchi chose to play white in the sudden-death game. Duda obtained a clear advantage, but found himself running seriously short of time against an opponent known for his speed in rapid and blitz chess. Despite having to rely on the one-second increment, the Polish star managed to convert his advantage. He later described his victory as "lucky", given how little time he had left on the clock.

Ian Nepomniachtchi and Jan-Krzysztof Duda, two formidable GMs, played a hard-fought match | Photo: Michal Walusza
The remaining four brackets also produced their finalists:
Ninth place: Arjun Erigaisi defeated Jorden van Foreest in Armageddon and will face Haik Martirosyan, who beat Richard Rapport by 2–0 in sets.
Thirteenth place: Levon Aronian needed Armageddon to overcome Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and will meet Wesley So, who defeated Vincent Keymer 2–0.
Seventeenth place: Vladislav Artemiev advanced past Andrew Hong in Armageddon and will meet Magnus Carlsen, who defeated Bibisara Assaubayeva by 1½–½ in sets.
Twenty-first place: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu beat Nodirbek Abdusattorov 2–0 in an all-elite encounter and will face Abhimanyu Mishra, who also won both sets against Vaishali Rameshbabu.

Following the controversy surrounding Carlsen's decision not to play his final fast classic game against Assaubayeva on Tuesday, the Norwegian once again declined to appear for the last encounter on Wednesday. By that point, he had won all four blitz games, followed by a win and a draw in rapid, giving him a 10–2 lead. Since the final game was worth 8 points, a forfeit loss would leave the set tied at 10–10, enough for Carlsen to advance.

This time, however, he was not the only player to skip the final game. Richard Rapport, who had already lost his match against Haik Martirosyan, also failed to appear, as did Abhimanyu Mishra, who had secured victory against Vaishali before their fast classic encounter.

The fact that two other players followed Carlsen's example might reduce some of the criticism directed at the Norwegian, although the situation has also raised broader questions about the tournament's format and the obligation to play games once a match has been decided.
Bibisara Assaubayeva got to play eight blitz games and four rapid games against the best player in the world | Photo: Michal Walusza

Emil Sutovsky, who had strongly criticised Carlsen's decision on Tuesday, again expressed his disapproval. In a social media post, he argued that the leading figures in chess have a responsibility towards the sport's development. He noted that an ambitious project such as Total Chess depends on satisfying investors, sponsors and broadcasters, and questioned whether television networks would remain interested if important games were regularly left unplayed. In his view, growing chess requires a collective effort from all major stakeholders.

Mishra responded directly to Sutovsky, offering a different perspective. The 17-year-old first praised the organisers and described the tournament as an excellent initiative, but pointed out that the schedule had been particularly demanding, with seven games played each day during the knockout stage. Mishra also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the rating status of games played after a match had already been decided.

The episode has added another question for the organisers to consider ahead of the full Total Chess Tour in 2027, particularly regarding the combination of a demanding daily schedule, officially rated fast classic games and matches that can be decided before the final encounter.
